item.title: Minimum wage in Uri: requirements and implementation
item.description: In Switzerland, there is no federal minimum wage: for Uri, it is necessary to distinguish between cantonal regulations, the sectors concerned and collective agreements.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - There is no federal minimum wage in Switzerland. - Some cantons apply their own minimum. - In Uri, the applicable rules, sector and contract matter. - A collective bargaining agreement does not coincide with a cantonal minimum.
## Key facts - Federal level → no minimum wage - Scope → possible cantonal regulations and sector - Verification → requirements, controls and competent office - Maximum hours → 45 or 50 hours per week - Holidays → 4 weeks, 5 under 20 years - Maternity → 14 weeks at 80% via IPG - Paternity → 2 weeks - Cancellation → 1, 2 or 3 months depending on seniority
In Switzerland there is no federal minimum wage: some cantons have their own. This distinction is the starting point for reading the case of the Canton of Uri, where the question is not only which figure to indicate, but which regulation applies to the relationship and the sector concerned.
### Uri-specific verification
For the Canton of Uri, the verification concerns any applicable cantonal regulations, the sectors involved, the requirements, controls and the competent office. Without a general cantonal rule, the reference to be examined is the relevant collective agreement. The collective agreement and the cantonal minimum wage remain distinct plans: one concerns the agreement that regulates the relationship within its scope, the other a possibly applicable cantonal regulation.
To correctly read a busta paga svizzera, it is best to link the salary to the sector and the applicable text, not to extract a threshold from generic data. SECO-related employment information does not replace this cantonal verification. UST/BFS performs a statistical function and does not set rates: a statistic does not automatically become a minimum wage.
The data not to be confused is therefore the source of the rule. A limit set by the Canton, when applicable, should not be presented as a simple statistical indication; Likewise, a provision of the collective agreement should not be transformed into a federal minimum. The distinction also guides the control of the competent office.
National labor standards also remain valid. The maximum working time is 45 hours per week for industry, offices and sales, and 50 hours in other sectors. The minimum holidays are four weeks, five for those under 20 years old. Maternity leave lasts 14 weeks at 80% via IPG, while paternity leave lasts two weeks. The notice periods are one month in the first year, two from the second to the ninth and three from the tenth. These rules do not indicate a minimum amount for Uri, but define the basic framework with which to read an employment relationship and the related remuneration. The practical comparison does not end with any threshold that may apply to the employment relationship. There are differences between salary, deductions and recurring expenses that change how a job offer in the Canton of Uri should be assessed. To avoid confusing a salary limit with a deduction, it is advisable to consider the items separately.
The same principle applies when comparing offers. A threshold that may apply, mandatory contributions and the insurance premium are governed by different rules: keeping them separate avoids attributing to the minimum wage an effect that instead belongs to social security or insurance.
### From the stated salary to deductions
| Item | Data to consider | | --- | --- | | AVS/AHV (AVS/AI/IPG) | 5.3% payable by the employee; 10.6% overall including the employer | | AD/AC | 1.1% up to an annual maximum | | LAINF/LAA | 0.7–1.5% depending on the sector | | LPP/BVG | 7%, 10%, 15% and 18% on the coordinated salary |
The percentages are not a minimum wage: they are contributions on salary and affect the amount available. For LPP/BVG, the bands indicated are 7% between ages 25 and 34, 10% between 35 and 44, 15% between 45 and 54, and 18% from age 55 up to the reference age. LAINF/LAA varies according to the sector. When comparing two hypothetical conditions, the same stated remuneration may therefore be accompanied by different items when the age relevant to LPP/BVG or the sector changes.
### The cost that does not come through the payslip
LAMal/KVG must be kept separate. For residents, health insurance is mandatory and must be taken out within three months of arrival. Premiums are per capita, vary by canton and region, and are neither a tax nor a salary contribution. Premium reductions follow cantonal rules.
This distinction changes how the cost of living is assessed. In a hypothetical scenario, the salary under an employment relationship can first be compared with the social-security items and then with the LAMal premium, without adding the two categories together as if they were the same deduction. To broaden the comparison, costo della vita in Svizzera can be used; for pension effects, the guide to pensione AVS/LPP. The result does not establish what the cantonal minimum is, but helps clarify what remains available after the different components.

### Five operational steps
1. Identify the employment relationship. Compare the available contract and payslip, noting the Canton of Uri, the sector and the scheduled working hours. This avoids using a salary reference unrelated to the employment relationship. 2. Check the cantonal rules. Check whether any rule of Uri covers that sector, what requirements it sets, how checks are organized and which competent office must be involved. The reference should be sought in the canton’s official source. 3. Separate the collective agreement. If there is no applicable cantonal minimum, check the relevant collective agreement and keep it separate from the cantonal rules. The question is not merely which figure appears, but which source makes it applicable. 4. Reconstruct the remuneration. Read the AVS/AI/IPG, AD/AC, LAINF/LAA and LPP/BVG items according to the data in the source. LAMal/KVG should not be included among wage contributions; for a resident, it remains compulsory insurance with a three-month deadline from arrival. 5. Note the other deadlines. Check maximum working hours, holidays, maternity, paternity and termination notice as elements separate from the minimum wage. If a difference emerges, retain the link between sector, applicable rule, check and competent office.

For the case of Uri, this information does not replace checking the cantonal rules and collective agreement. Nor can a statistical figure be turned into a legal threshold.

In August, the Municipality of Como issued 1.259 fines in 31 days, for a total of 102.738 euros. The figure is accompanied by the daily amount of 3.322 euros. The penalties were recorded through the work of municipal police officers and auxiliary personnel.
### The figure recorded by the Municipality
The text presents the figure within Como's tourism context. Hotel stays are one of the indicators mentioned; the other is the number and amount of fines issued to vehicles with foreign license plates, which usually go unpaid. The reports concern cars left in unacceptable spots and positions. The phenomenon is not limited to summer: cases have also been reported outside the summer season.
Among the foreign license plates, the source specifically mentions Swiss ones. For Swiss motorists in Como, the connection is therefore tangible: the issue is the parking of a vehicle with a foreign license plate and the collection of the municipal fine. The issue is described as longstanding and linked to the difficulty of cross-border collection, as well as the high costs of pursuing offenders.
Over time, many fines issued to vehicles with foreign license plates, especially Swiss ones, have remained unpaid within the prescribed deadlines. Available estimates indicate that the share of ignored notices exceeds 80%. This results in a difference between the amount of fines issued and the amount actually collected, according to the framework outlined by the source.

The resolution provides for an allocation to the allowance for doubtful debts for receivables of doubtful and difficult collection.

2. If a ticket is issued, separate the amount reported on the document from historical estimates about collection. The value of the individual notice should be read on the document itself, while the percentage above 80% concerns the historical picture cited by the source.

## The network remains central The St. Gallen Cantonal Bank (SGKB) confirms the central role of its network of 37 physical branches. This is the position expressed by CEO Christian Schmid in an interview published by Finanz und Wirtschaft, while the Swiss banking landscape is described as evolving.
Schmid, 57, linked the role of branches to proximity to the local area, networks of contacts and roots in the region. For the bank, this presence is a strength, and no downsizing of the network is planned.
> The bank considers proximity to the local area, relationships built locally and regional roots to be its strength and categorically rules out any downsizing of its branch network.
### The main account as a goal Schmid approaches competition from neobanks, including Revolut, with a certain calm. The manager identifies defending its status as the main bank as the goal. The reasoning concerns the number-one current account: whoever holds it, according to Schmid, remains the main financial point of reference in the customer’s life.
The executive’s profile includes a doctorate earned at HSG, the University of St. Gallen. In the interview, this element accompanies the assessments of competition and the bank’s position in the region.

The source does not preview any other details of the plan, but reports that the operating model aimed at the domestic market in German-speaking Switzerland, Germany, institutional investors and external asset managers is producing excellent results, according to management.

## Key facts - Topic → continuing education in the Canton of Lucerne - Competence → Canton and cantonal offices - Requirements → cantonal rules - Deadlines → official Canton source - Amounts → official Canton source
In the Canton of Lucerne, continuing education follows a cantonal framework. For anyone seeking a contribution, the points to verify are the recognized programs, requirements, application deadlines and amount provided for under the applicable rules. The operational reference is not a national list of amounts or deadlines: it is the Canton’s rules that guide the verification.
### The scope of the measure
The first step is to check the Canton’s official portal and the responsible cantonal office. These sources indicate the requirements applicable to the training program and the applicant. Since measures for energy, building permits and continuing education aid are regulated and managed at cantonal level, the relevant responsibility should not automatically be attributed to a federal authority.
The boundary also serves to correctly interpret the names of the institutions. The Swiss tax system has three levels: direct federal tax, cantonal tax and municipal tax. AFC/ESTV manages direct federal tax and VAT, while the cantonal administrations handle cantonal and municipal taxation. UFAS/BSV concerns social security, including AVS/AHV, AI and LPP/BVG; it does not set taxes. Continuing education, on the other hand, is indicated by the source among the benefits and services subject to cantonal rules.
The same criterion avoids other overlaps. LAMal/KVG is compulsory health insurance for residents, with per-capita premiums, and is neither a tax nor a wage contribution. AVS/AHV and LPP/BVG belong to social security, not to the procedure for requesting a training contribution. The reference for Lucerne therefore remains the cantonal one indicated by the official source.
Minimum wage and cost of living also do not alone define access to the contribution. They may factor into the personal assessment of a course, but requirements, deadlines and amounts remain those indicated by the cantonal rules. The fact that the application has a deadline and an amount to be verified rules out the idea of automatic support that is the same for every course or applicant.
Anyone who wants to separate the contribution from personal taxation can start with the guide to dichiarazione delle imposte: the link concerns their own tax situation, does not certify recognition of the program and does not replace the cantonal office. For those who live or work in Switzerland, the distinction between cantonal rules and federal jurisdiction creates a sequence of checks. It is not enough to find a course consistent with one's work: before including a contribution in the budget, it is necessary to verify whether the program is recognized, which requirements apply, by what deadline the application must be submitted and what amount Lucerne's rules provide.

The table serves to avoid confusing four pieces of information: the program concerns the offering; the requirements, the applicant; the deadline, the timing of the application; the amount, the support. Looking for only a figure leaves the other checks open.
The practical comparison is between two sequences. In the first, one chooses the course and only then looks for the contribution. In that situation, it is not yet clear whether the program is recognized, whether the person meets the requirements, whether the application is timely or what amount may be taken into account. In the second, one starts from the Canton’s official source, checks the pathway and reads the procedure before relying on the support. The second sequence reduces the risk of building the budget on unverified information.
Hypothetical scenario: a worker considering continuing education can separate two questions. The first concerns the pathway and its recognition; the second concerns their own position with respect to the contribution. Only the second leads to the cantonal application. If either check is missing, the cost of the course cannot automatically be considered covered.
Personal budgeting should be considered separately. costo della vita in Svizzera may affect the choice of training, but it does not establish the conditions for the contribution. The same applies to the minimum wage: the existence of a cantonal wage threshold alone does not create a right to continuing education. AVS/AHV and LPP/BVG concern social security, while LAMal/KVG concerns mandatory health insurance; none of these references replaces verification specific to Lucerne.
To guide the search, the criterion is jurisdiction: training contribution through the cantonal office; direct federal tax and VAT through AFC/ESTV; social security through UFAS/BSV. This separation prevents using a tax calculator or a social security guide as proof of eligibility for the support.

## In brief - US tariffs on goods produced with forced labor from July 24, 2026 - Federal vote on war materiel on November 29, 2026 - Resignation of State Secretary Helene Budliger Artieda at the end of March 2027

On July 24, 2026, the United States introduced new trade measures, applying variable additional duties of up to 12.5% on goods imported from Switzerland, based on investigations into forced labor conducted under the Trade Act of 1974. Unlike previous periods, compliance with forced labor regulations, as outlined in Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974, becomes a direct evaluation parameter for market access. This situation requires constant attention from national economic operators. On the political front, the vote on November 29, 2026, regarding the Federal Act on War Material is part of a legislative review process that directly involves Parliament and the Federal Council. The resignation announced on September 16, 2026, by Helene Budliger Artieda, scheduled for the end of March 2027, marks a transition phase for the leadership of the State Secretariat. The creation of a succession committee ensures operational continuity during a period characterized by complex challenges, including the implementation of sanctions against Russia, supported by the Federal Council since February 28, 2022. The solidity of the organization is guaranteed by the presence of over 900 employees who work daily to monitor the national and foreign economy. SECO's efficiency in coordinating the various strategic directorates remains the cornerstone for managing the repercussions of such decisions on the country's economic life, balancing the needs of international compliance with Swiss legislative priorities regarding exports and foreign policy.

Axpo has begun construction in Suhr, in the canton of Aargau, of a solar plant on arable land. The project has a precise objective: to show whether agricultural use and electricity production can coexist on the same area.
### An area divided between energy and agriculture
The plant will have a power output of 600 kilowatts peak, indicated by the abbreviation kWp. The experimental area measures 2,8 hectares, but the modules will be installed on 1,2 hectares. They will be positioned approximately three metres above the ground and can be oriented according to the season.
The area underneath will not be taken away from cultivation: it will continue to be used for agriculture. This is the operational focus of the experiment, because the project maintains both the productive function of the field and the energy function of the modules in the same space.
### The comparison entrusted to FiBL
Axpo, the canton of Aargau and FiBL, the Research Institute of Organic Agriculture based in Frick, are collaborating on the project. The institute will assess the effects of the modules on yields, water balance and biodiversity.
The results from the area equipped with the modules will be compared with those obtained in a nearby field without panels. Emmi will purchase all the solar energy generated and use it directly at its plant in Suhr.
Axpo will be responsible for both the construction and operation of the plant; the farmer who already managed the field will continue to cultivate it. FiBL will handle the field research, Axpo the technical aspects, the farmer the cultivation and Emmi the use of the electricity. In Suhr, the project thus brings cultivation, business activity and electricity generation together on the same area. The practical value of the project lies not only in the 600 kWp. It lies in the fact that the same area is being studied as an agricultural field and as a surface for solar modules. item.title: Referendum against new nuclear power plants in Switzerland
item.description: More than 131.800 signatures delivered to Bern by SP, Verdi, GLP and part of Centro to maintain the ban on nuclear power; vote possible on February 28, 2027.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - More than 131.800 signatures against new nuclear plants - SP, Greens, GLP and part of the Centre in Bern - Winter shortfall is around 6,8 TWh - Possible vote on February 28, 2027
## Key facts - Signatures → more than 131.800 - Location and parties → SP, the Greens, GLP and part of the Centre - Nuclear share → just under 30% of domestic electricity production - Winter shortfall → around 6,8 TWh in 2025–26 - Possible vote → February 28, 2027
### The submission of the signatures More than 131.800 signatures were submitted in Bern by an alliance of left-wing and centrist parties that wants to prevent Switzerland from lifting the ban on building new nuclear power plants. Greenpeace reported on the submission, carried out on Tuesday by representatives of the Socialist Party, the Greens, the Green Liberals and part of the Centre.
The political objective is to maintain the ban already in force. Lisa Mazzone, president of the Greens, described nuclear energy as an outdated and expensive technology that leaves future generations highly radioactive waste. Her position places the signature drive within the debate between investment in renewables and a return to nuclear power.
The discussion starts from a fact concerning the national electricity system as a whole. Nuclear energy currently accounts for just under 30% of Switzerland's domestic electricity production. During the winter months, however, the country cannot produce enough electricity to meet demand and relies on imports. The shortfall was around 6,8 TWh in the winter of 2025–26, equivalent to around one fifth of the country's winter consumption.
### The two positions on winter Vanessa Gassler-Meury, a member of the committee of the Stop the Blackout initiative, argues that the problem will worsen when the existing nuclear power plants are shut down. In her view, renewables alone are not enough: solar power is intermittent, while nuclear provides a constant supply. For this reason, nuclear energy would be particularly important in winter, when reliable, low-carbon electricity is needed.
The pro-solar camp, by contrast, emphasizes the capacity that is already growing. Last winter, solar energy produced more than 2 TWh, an amount equivalent to the additional winter electricity production expected from the planned expansion of hydropower by 2040. Renewable energy supporters fear that lifting the ban would slow investment in solar power. Jürg Grossen, president of the Green Liberals, submitted a parliamentary motion to maintain solar subsidies. Priska Wismer-Felder, a National Council member from the Centre in Lucerne, supports the referendum and calls for resources to be focused on renewables. If the ballot goes ahead, the vote could be held as early as February 28, 2027. ## What's at stake for the electricity system
For anyone living or working in Switzerland, the practical point is to distinguish three levels: domestic production already available, the winter shortfall and the additional capacity expected from renewables. The source does not put these figures on the same footing, and this is precisely where part of the political debate lies.
### Different numbers, different questions
| Measure | Reported figure | What it indicates | |---|---|---| | Nuclear share | Just under 30% of domestic production | The current weight of nuclear energy | | Winter shortfall | Around 6,8 TWh in 2025–26 | Reliance on imports in the cold months | | Solar energy | More than 2 TWh last winter | A growing renewable contribution | | Hydropower | Expected additional winter production by 2040 | A planned expansion of renewables |
A nuclear share of just under 30% describes the current weight of the technology in domestic production. The 6,8 TWh shortfall, on the other hand, describes what is missing in winter relative to demand and is covered by imports. The more than 2 TWh produced by solar last winter measure renewable capacity already in place; the figure linked to hydropower concerns an additional target by 2040.
This distinction avoids two automatic conclusions. Solar growth is not presented as eliminating the winter shortfall. At the same time, the nuclear share alone does not resolve the choice of how to manage the closure of existing plants. Stop the Blackout's position focuses on the continuity of winter supply; referendum supporters focus on renewables and fear that new plants will slow investment in solar.
The debate also has a resource-allocation dimension. For Priska Wismer-Felder, opening the door to nuclear construction now would mean spreading investments too thinly; Jürg Grossen has called for maintaining solar subsidies. The practical path for a reader is primarily informational: the source describes the submission of the signatures and indicates a possible voting date, but does not yet present an outcome. To avoid confusing the steps, proceed as follows.
### Five useful steps
1. Consider February 28, 2027, the nearest date indicated for a possible consultation, not a certain date: the source specifies that the vote depends on whether the referendum proceeds. 2. Identify the choice under discussion: retain the ban on new nuclear power plants or repeal it. This is not the same as already knowing the outcome of the vote. 3. item.description: The referendum on the proposal will be held on November 29.

## TL;DR - The referendum on the proposal will be held on November 29. - Standard VAT: from 8,1% to 8,5%; hotels: from 3,8% to 4%. - 2035 deficit: almost CHF 5 billion without an increase; around CHF 3 billion with one. - In December: an extra for around 2,5 million people.
## Key facts - Measure → VAT increase for the 13th annual pension payment - Referendum → November 29 - 2035 deficit without increase → almost CHF 5 billion a year - 2035 deficit with increase → about CHF 3 billion a year - Reserves without increase → 50% of annual spending in 2035 - Reserves with increase → 70% of annual spending in 2035 - Standard rate → from 8,1% to 8,5% - Special hotel rate → from 3,8% to 4%
On November 29, Swiss voters will decide in a referendum whether to finance the 13th annual payment of the state pension through a VAT increase. Elisabeth Baume-Schneider, minister of social affairs, defended the proposal at a press conference in Bern, as reported by RTS. She said that, without additional revenue, the state pension scheme would come under increasing financial strain.
According to government estimates, a rejection would bring the pension fund to an annual deficit of almost CHF 5 billion by 2035. With the VAT increase, the deficit would fall to about CHF 3 billion. Reserves risk falling below the legal minimum of one year's spending in 2027.
In 2035, without the increase, reserves would cover 50% of annual spending; with a yes vote on the measure, they would reach 70%. The referendum is scheduled shortly before the first payment of the 13th pension payment, which will arrive in December.
The extra payment will cost CHF 4,2 billion, with CHF 1,4 billion covered by the higher VAT. Next December, about 2,5 million people will receive it. For those following pensione, the vote therefore combines the choice on funding with the first payment.
Baume-Schneider describes Parliament’s package as a moderate, socially acceptable compromise: the standard VAT rate would rise from 8,1% to 8,5%, while the special rate for hotels would increase from 3,8% to 4%. The reduced rate on essentials such as food and medicines would stay at 2,6%, and health insurance premiums would remain exempt from VAT.
### Government, Parliament and opposition The minister argues that the unchanged reduced rate protects lower incomes and that all revenue goes to social security. The Federal Council and Parliament see the measure as a sharing of the cost between generations. The parliamentary minority, however, fears a decline in purchasing power. The PLR/FDP, which has campaigned against the proposal since the end of September, prefers spending cuts and structural reforms, including raising the retirement age. Baume-Schneider said that the latter option would require Parliament and voters and expressed confidence in a yes vote. ## What changes in practice
The proposal divides the fiscal impact differently depending on the spending item. This is where the referendum choice affects everyday life: the standard rate and the rate for hotels would rise, while essential goods and health insurance premiums receive different treatment. PLR/FDP sees the increase as additional pressure on families and small and medium-sized enterprises; Baume-Schneider presents it as a socially acceptable compromise.
### Four treatments to distinguish
| Item | Rule set out in the proposal | |---|---| | Standard rate | from 8,1% to 8,5% | | Special rate for hotels | from 3,8% to 4% | | Essential goods | 2,6%, no increase | | Health insurance premiums | no VAT |
For a household budget, protection is not general but concentrated on essential goods. The unchanged reduced rate is the argument the minister uses to argue that she can contain the burden on lower incomes. The opposition's criticism takes the opposite view: according to opponents, higher VAT would erode purchasing power when it affects spending subject to the standard rate. The reference to costo della vita therefore hinges on comparing items, not on a single percentage applied to everything.
For small and medium-sized enterprises, the political issue is similar. The PLR/FDP campaign argues that higher VAT would add pressure on businesses and families and proposes spending cuts. The Federal Council and Parliament reply that the revenue would be allocated directly to social security and that the financing would be distributed across generations.
The pension comparison, however, remains decisive. Even with the increase, the projected annual deficit for 2035 would still be around CHF 3 billion: the measure reduces the gap, but does not eliminate it. Without new revenue, the deficit would rise to almost CHF 5 billion and reserves would cover 50% of annual expenditure, compared with 70% with a yes vote. The one-year expenditure threshold, at risk in 2027, makes the timetable a concrete element of the choice.
The retirement-age alternative does not provide, in the minister's description, an immediate solution: it would require approval from Parliament and voters. The referendum therefore pits a VAT increase against the pursuit of structural reforms or cuts.

### Four operational steps
1. Identify the political question. The referendum concerns the proposal to use higher VAT revenues to finance the annual thirteenth pension payment. The retirement age, on the other hand, belongs to the alternatives discussed by opponents: changing it would require Parliament and voters.
2. Separate expenditure items. In your own budget, it is advisable to distinguish what falls under the standard rate, hotels, essential goods and health insurance premiums. item.description: Mastercard will introduce the feature in Switzerland from 2027 New cards will support it from February 2027 New or replaced terminals: technology by May
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Mastercard will introduce the feature in Switzerland from 2027 - New cards will support it from February 2027 - New or replaced terminals: technology by May - Europe: up to 200 euro per purchase, paying with PIN
## Key facts - Function → payment with Mastercard without internet - Launch → from 2027 in Europe and Switzerland - Card requested → new card - Terminal → power supply - Limit indicated → up to 200 euros per purchase in Europe - Verification → directly between card and terminal - Method → PIN - Limit → established by the bank
Starting from 2027, Mastercard will gradually introduce a function in Europe and Switzerland that will allow consumers to pay even when the internet is not available, if there is electricity. The declared objective is to prevent the cashless payment system from stalling during widespread disruptions.
A Mastercard spokeswoman indicated this to the AWP agency. The effect will concern ordinary purchases in supermarkets, petrol stations and pharmacies: if the internet connection drops, the payment can still be verified directly between the card and the terminal.
### The two introduction deadlines
For the consumer, the first date is February 2027. From that month all newly issued cards will have to support the function. To use it, however, you will need a new card: the technology is therefore not presented as an update applicable to the card already in possession.
The second step concerns the terminals. By May, all newly installed or replaced ones will have to be equipped with the corresponding technology. The introduction will therefore be gradual, with the adaptation linked to new card issues and interventions on payment devices.
The technical prerequisite remains the electrical power supply to the terminal. In the absence of internet, the customer will pay with the PIN. For Europe, Mastercard indicates amounts of up to 200 euros per purchase, while specifying that the limit is established by the bank. As soon as the connection is available again, the payment will then be processed.
The payment is not described as an operation suspended without verification: during the outage the card and the terminal carry out the check, while the processing arrives after the connection is restored. The source therefore separates the moment of verification from that of processing.
The company links the news to a problem that already emerged during the electricity blackout in Spain and Portugal in April 2025, when millions of people were unable to pay by card. The feature described for 2027, however, concerns the interruption of the internet and does not eliminate the electricity requirement. For those using a Mastercard in Switzerland, the crucial distinction is between the internet going down and a lack of electricity. The announced feature concerns the first scenario, but only if the terminal remains powered. Electricity is therefore not a detail: it is the technical prerequisite identified by Mastercard.
### The terminal is the real test
| Condition | Planned verification | |---|---| | Internet down and terminal powered | The card and terminal verify the payment directly; the PIN is used. | | Connection restored | The payment is then processed. |
The first scenario is the one that directly affects anyone paying in a store: the internet is not working, but the terminal remains powered. In this situation, verification takes place directly between the card and terminal, and the PIN becomes the required method. The process does not depend on the network returning immediately: the payment is processed when the connection returns.
The limit should be interpreted without making automatic conversions. The source refers to amounts of up to 200 euro per purchase for Europe and adds that the bank sets the limit. No threshold in Swiss francs is specified. For a possible comparison between the two currencies, comparatore CHF/EUR can be used, but the result does not replace the limit set by the bank.
The power blackout in Spain and Portugal in April 2025 shows what can happen when the power supply fails: millions of people were unable to pay by card. The feature announced for 2027 is instead designed to keep cashless payment traffic active during internet disruptions, always with the terminal powered.
The case of Latvia provides further practical evidence. The technology is already operational in Denmark, Sweden, Estonia and Latvia. When, in August, the country was hit by one of the most severe storms in its history, shops equipped with emergency generators were able to continue accepting card payments.

## Key facts - Subject → easing of the law on war materiel - Date → November 29, 2026 - Countries concerned → close partners with comparable rules - Condition → exports possible even during an armed conflict - Ukraine → excluded from the new rules
### The federal vote and the proposed amendment
On November 29, 2026, the Swiss population will vote on a controversial easing of the law on war materiel. The reform establishes a separate regime for certain countries that Switzerland considers close partners and that apply export rules similar to those in Switzerland.
If these countries were involved in an armed conflict, Swiss exports to them could nevertheless be authorized. The wording therefore describes differentiated treatment linked to the type of partner and the comparability of the rules, not an indiscriminate opening toward all war zones.
The vote comes after criticism directed at Switzerland for having prevented Germany and other countries from re-exporting Swiss war materiel to Ukraine. According to the source, that decision prompted several European states to sever ties with Swiss manufacturers. The link between the political debate and the manufacturing sector is therefore explicit: the choice regarding the law also concerns Swiss manufacturers' relations with other countries.
Ukraine, however, is not among the states that would benefit from the new rules. This element defines the scope of the reform: the case that fueled the criticism does not coincide with the list of potential beneficiaries. For those observing the effects on industrial employment, the reference to manufacturers and their relations with other countries can be considered alongside the search for aziende che assumono, without turning the vote into an employment forecast.
### Neutrality, openness or isolationism
The discussion is not limited to the delivery of weapons. Swiss neutrality, the source writes, sparks heated debate in times of crisis and raises a fundamental question: openness or isolationism?
The comments cited reveal opposing positions. One contribution argues that a country cannot truly be considered neutral if it provides direct or indirect support through personnel, information, operational bases or the sale of weapons. Another position states that arms exports have no place in a neutral country, but that neutrality must have limits when some states violate international law.
Another comment, by contrast, defends the need to consider the consequences of the possible disappearance of the arms industry: loss of jobs and know-how, higher costs to maintain the armed forces, and an even lower position in the priority of supplies. The vote thus puts before the people not only a rule on exports, but also a choice about the concrete meaning of Swiss neutrality. ## What could change for Switzerland
The reform links two different choices: deciding which countries Swiss war materiel may be sent to and establishing how much neutrality should weigh when a partner is involved in a conflict. The first choice concerns the scope of authorizations; the second concerns the political interpretation of Swiss neutrality. Keeping the two questions separate helps avoid attributing effects to the reform that the text does not foresee.

| Step | Practical reading | |---|---| | Case that fueled criticism | Germany and other countries have not been able to re-export Swiss war materiel to Ukraine; several European states have severed relations with Swiss manufacturers. | | Proposed rule | Some close partners, with comparable rules, could receive authorizations even if involved in an armed conflict. | | Explicit limitation | Ukraine is not among the states that would benefit from the new rules. | | Industrial argument | One comment points to jobs, know-how, the costs of maintaining the armed forces, and supply priorities. |

The criterion indicated by the source is narrower: what matters is the relationship with Switzerland and the comparability of export rules. For a manufacturer, the change would therefore alter the range of countries for which a delivery may be authorized; it would not automatically turn the Ukrainian case into an admissible case.
The second aspect is neutrality. Part of the debate considers arms sales incompatible with neutrality, especially when direct or indirect assistance includes personnel, information, operational bases, or war materiel. Another position instead calls for recognizing limits to neutrality when a state violates international law. In the text, these interpretations are presented as opposing arguments.
The position in favor of the arms industry’s existence points to very concrete consequences: if the industry disappeared, jobs and know-how would be lost; maintaining the armed forces would become extremely costly and Switzerland would fall even further behind in supply priorities. The opposing position places the moral limit of exports at the center. The point for anyone following national politics is to choose which of these effects should carry more weight. 2. Recipients. Possible involvement in an armed conflict does not eliminate, for these countries, the possibility of authorization.

## TL;DR - 1.587 voluntary reports in one week - New high since at least the beginning of 2025 - 41% of companies surveyed by Deloitte have suffered an attack - 280 notifications involving critical infrastructure from January to August
## Key facts - Authority → Federal Office for Cybersecurity (UFCS) - Record reports → 1.587 in one week - Previous record → 1.353, one month earlier - Notification obligation → in force since April 2025 - Deloitte study → 281 board members; 41% of companies affected
In the past week, the Federal Office for Cybersecurity (UFCS) recorded 1.587 voluntary reports, the highest weekly figure at least since the beginning of 2025. This figure exceeds the previous record, which stood at 1.353 reports and had been reached just one month earlier, by more than 17%.
The figure comes in a Swiss context marked by attacks targeting the online platform Ricardo, the federal pension fund Publica, and the aerospace company Beyond Gravity. Distinct from one another, these incidents have brought the cybersecurity of companies and institutions back into the spotlight.
### The record does not equate to damage
The majority of reports received by the UFCS concern phishing attempts, scams and unsolicited messages. For this reason, the record cannot be read as a count of successful attacks: not all reports correspond to successful cyberattacks or incidents that caused damage.
Between January and August, the UFCS recorded 280 reports of cyber incidents in critical infrastructures subject to the notification obligation. In the April–August period, there were 173 reports, compared with the 104 recorded in the same period of the previous year. The notification obligation has been in force since April 2025.
An additional indicator is provided by a Deloitte study released in mid-September, based on interviews with 281 members of the boards of directors of small, medium-sized and large companies. The survey found that 41% of the companies involved had already suffered a cyberattack: compared with three years ago, the share has increased by 13 percentage points. Anyone consulting aziende che assumono will therefore find different information: here, cyber exposure is measured, not seat availability.
Raphael Hauser, Abraxas's head of cybersecurity, argues that cybercriminals are increasingly combining vulnerabilities in widely used software, stolen login credentials and techniques for manipulating employees. The expert discussed this at the beginning of October in an interview with the specialized portal Swisscybersecurity.net. Experts also warn that artificial intelligence could further facilitate attacks. ## How to read the data
The first useful data point for anyone working at a Swiss company is the distinction between an alert and a successful attack. A phishing message or a scam can generate a report even when it causes no damage. The increase in reports therefore describes the events that came to the authority's attention; on its own, it does not make it possible to calculate how many systems were compromised. This distinction prevents a statistical peak from automatically becoming a measure of losses.
### Three indicators, three interpretations
| Indicator | Correct interpretation | Limitation of the data | | Voluntary reports | Include phishing, scams and unwanted messages | Are not equivalent to successful attacks | | Critical infrastructure | Concern incidents subject to mandatory notification | Do not represent every threat to companies | | Deloitte survey | Covers companies that report having suffered an attack | Does not quantify the economic damage |
The second point concerns critical infrastructure. The series of incidents subject to notification and that of voluntary reports should not be added together automatically to obtain a total number of attacks in Switzerland: they describe different categories. For a board of directors, this distinction is crucial when comparing internal alerts with public data.
The same caution is needed for the Deloitte survey. The percentage recorded measures the experience reported by the companies involved, not the weekly number of reports received by the UFCS. The sample includes members of the boards of directors of small, medium-sized and large companies; the result describes a proportion of exposed companies, not the flow of incidents reported to the authority.
Raphael Hauser's analysis adds an operational element: vulnerabilities in widely used software, stolen credentials and the manipulation of employees can be exploited together. In a generic scenario, the visible message may be just one step in a broader chain. This does not make it possible to automatically attribute all vectors to a single case.
Finally, artificial intelligence introduces a forward-looking warning. Experts indicate that it could make attacks easier to carry out. For those consulting annunci di lavoro, the topic therefore remains distinct from employment: here, the cyber exposure of companies is measured.

## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare CHF-EUR exchange options and banks for cross-border workers. ## From reading to action
The source information enables a cautious operational sequence, without conflating different categories. The starting point is not the absolute number of reports, but the nature of the signal and the technical or human vector described by the experts.
### Four steps for a company
1. Classify the event. Separate phishing, scams and unwanted messages from a successful cyberattack. The distinction prevents every alert from being considered already confirmed damage.
2. Examine the combination. Review the three elements identified by Raphael Hauser: vulnerabilities in widely used software, stolen access credentials and employee manipulation. They are described as tools used with increasing frequency and combined with one another. The review must therefore remain broad, without attributing an unproven vector to a single incident.
3. Establish the reporting regime. If the activity falls within critical infrastructure, keep incidents subject to the notification requirement separate from voluntary reports received by the UFCS. The relevant point in time to consider is April 2025, when the requirement came into force.
4. Consider artificial intelligence. The experts warn that it can make attacks easier to carry out. It should therefore be treated as a factor to monitor, not as proof that an attack has already occurred.
For management, the Deloitte survey can serve as an external benchmark for companies' exposure. However, it does not replace an examination of the individual case: a percentage reported by members of boards of directors and a report received by the UFCS belong to different levels. Internal records should keep at least the type of message, the presence of a successful attack and any connection to critical infrastructure separate. This framework follows the distinctions provided by the source without adding a technical procedure not described there.
The timeline also needs to be read correctly. The record for one week, the series of incidents subject to notification and the survey published in mid-September have different observation periods. Comparing them as though they were the same indicator would lead to an incorrect conclusion.

## TL;DR - In September, the SECO index fell to -35,8 points - The figure fell by 3,0 points compared with August - Job security fell to -60,6 - This is the first decrease in the indicator since last March
## Key facts - Overall indicator in September → -35,8 points - Overall indicator in August → -32,8 points - Expected economic development → from -36,4 to -42,5 - Financial situation in past months → from -38,8 to -42,3 - Job security → from -54,3 to -60,6 - Expected prices over the next twelve months → from 113,3 to 115,6 - Average 2023-2026 → -37,3
In September, the Swiss consumer confidence index stood at -35,8 points. Based on the survey by the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), the figure fell by 3,0 points from the -32,8 recorded in August, marking the first decline since last March. Compared with the previous year, the decrease reached 0,7 points, while the index remains slightly above the 2023-2026 average, set at -37,3. The deterioration is accompanied by more pronounced pessimism about the personal situation, the perception of high prices, and concerns about job security.
### The components of confidence
The decline affects several components. Expectations for the country's economic performance fell from -36,4 to -42,5, well below the multi-year average of -34,3. The assessment of the personal financial situation also worsened: the figure for the months just past fell from -38,8 to -42,3, while that for the coming months fell from -29,6 to -31,0. As for major purchases, the time continues to be considered unfavorable, with the sub-index falling from -26,3 to -27,3.
The item concerning job security fell from -54,3 to -60,6, remaining the clearest signal. The figure remains well below the average for the last three years, at -34,7.
### Prices and index construction
Prices also enter the picture. The sub-index for past developments rises from 122,5 to 129,3; that for expectations over the next twelve months from 113,3 to 115,6. For the next five years, the figure falls from 109,2 to 105,8, while remaining very high. The scale produces positive balances when the majority of consumers perceive a price increase.
The survey has been conducted since 1972: in the past it was quarterly, whereas recently it has been monthly. To ensure fair regional representation, the Ticino sample is deliberately larger and participants are asked fourteen questions. The response options range from much better (+2) to markedly worse (-2), including better, no change, and worse. Each question yields a sub-index; the overall climate corresponds to the average of four indicators: economic situation in the coming months, financial situation in the past months and the coming months, favorable time for major purchases. The September figure should be read by separating the aspects measured by the survey. The -35,8 is not the change in a single expense: it summarizes four sub-indices used for the overall climate and is accompanied by other signals on prices and job security. For people living in Switzerland, this distinction makes it possible to turn the national figure into a concrete question about their own budget, without confusing a collective perception with a personal figure.

The three price readings do not describe the same phase. The value relating to the past rises from 122,5 to 129,3: the balance is more positive in the assessment of price increases already perceived. The one for the next twelve months rises from 113,3 to 115,6. The series for the next five years, however, falls from 109,2 to 105,8, while remaining at very high levels.

item.description: The U.S. vote on November 3 could weigh on the Swiss economy.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - The U.S. election on November 3 may weigh on the Swiss economy. - In 2025, bilateral trade reached 293 billion. - Three outcomes concern tariffs, the dollar and financial markets. - Polymarket estimates a 93% chance for the Democrats in the House.
## Key facts - Date → November 3 - Seats → 435 in the House and 35 of the 100 Senate seats - Trade 2025 → 293 billion dollars, approximately 243 billion francs - S&P 500 → always up over the 100 days; average gain of 10% over 75 years - Polymarket, House → 93% for a Democratic victory - Polymarket, Senate → approximately 65% for a Democratic victory - Reuters/Ipsos → 44% Democrats and 37% Republicans among registered voters
On November 3, the United States will renew Congress. Midterm elections concern not only Donald Trump's political future: they can also affect the Swiss economy through tariffs, the dollar and financial markets. The trade relationship is significant: in 2025, the total value of trade in goods and services between the two countries was 293 billion dollars, equivalent to approximately 243 billion francs.
### Three political scenarios The election will fill all 435 seats in the House of Representatives; in the Senate, 35 of 100 seats will be up for election. The first possibility is a Democratic victory in both chambers, with the president's room for maneuver severely limited. The second scenario sees the Democrats prevail in the House, while the Republicans retain control of the Senate. The third is the Republican majority being maintained, which would make it easier for Trump to pursue his economic agenda.
According to J. Safra Sarasin, a double Democratic majority could favor a “selective de-escalation” of trade tensions with allies. Trump would nevertheless retain the power to block measures with a veto and issue executive orders.
### Tariffs and exchange rates For Swiss companies, the most delicate issue is US tariffs. Santosh Brivio, an economist at Banca Migros, observes: “Tariffs are certainly no postcards bearing friendly greetings.” The barriers make exports more expensive and complicate planning, especially in pharmaceuticals, machinery manufacturing and watchmaking. If Congress were divided, existing tariffs would probably remain, while new measures would be more difficult; with a confirmed Republican majority, trade tensions could increase.
Lombard Odier believes that a gridlocked Congress could limit US public spending, lower interest rates and weaken the dollar, although less pressure on the US central bank could increase confidence in the currency. With a weak dollar, travel and purchases in the United States would cost Swiss consumers less; for exporters, revenues would generally be lower after conversion into francs. Clientis finally notes that, in the short term, fuel and heating will depend mainly on geopolitical tensions and oil. To track the exchange rate, comparatore CHF/EUR can be viewed alongside the data. ## Different effects on the Swiss budget The American vote does not have just one effect on the Swiss budget. The same political configuration can affect an exporting company, a family that makes purchases in the United States and anyone observing the financial markets differently. To assess the impact, it is useful to separate trade, exchange rates and investments.
### Three channels, three readings | Scenario | Trade | Exchange rates and markets | |---|---|---| | Democrats in both chambers | Possible selective reduction in tensions; veto power and executive orders remain. | Effects on the exchange rate are difficult to predict. | | Divided Congress | Existing tariffs will probably remain in force; new tariffs will be more difficult. | Public spending could be reduced, with lower interest rates and a weaker dollar; less pressure on the central bank could strengthen confidence in the currency. | | Confirmed Republican majority | Possible further trade escalation. | Trump can more easily continue the economic agenda; the effect on the dollar remains difficult to predict. |
For a Swiss company selling in the United States, tariffs and exchange rates must be considered together: tariffs raise the cost of exports and make planning more complex, while a weak dollar can reduce revenues once converted into francs. Pharmaceuticals, the machinery industry and watchmaking are the sectors identified as particularly exposed.
For consumers, the relationship is reversed. A weak dollar makes travel and purchases in the United States less expensive, but it does not provide a general explanation for every energy expense: according to Clientis, in the short term, fuel and heating are affected above all by geopolitical tensions and oil prices. Anyone following costo della vita in Svizzera should therefore distinguish between consumption linked to exchange rates and prices linked to energy.
On the investment front, Thomas Gitzel, chief economist at VP Bank, points out that for stock markets it is not decisive who gains or loses how many seats. Over the past 75 years, the S&P 500 index has gained ground in every 100-day window following midterm elections, with an average rise of 10%. History calls for caution: over the long term, corporate earnings, inflation and central-bank decisions matter. A highly contested result can also increase political tensions and volatility, especially after accusations of possible electoral fraud, unsupported by evidence, repeated by Trump.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare CHF-EUR exchange options and banks for cross-border workers. ## A practical check after the vote For those who live or work in Switzerland, the most concrete approach is to turn the date of November 3 into an orderly check. There is no need to anticipate the outcome: the consultation presents three configurations and different channels for trade, foreign exchange and markets. The following sequence separates the steps without adding forecasts.
### Five steps 1. Mark the date and the two chambers. On November 3, all 435 House seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are up for election. For the Senate, consider the results in individual states, described as decisive for the majority.
2. Classify the result. Use the three configurations described: Democrats in both chambers, a divided Congress or a confirmed Republican majority. This distinction serves to interpret tariffs and the economic agenda differently.
3. Check trade exposure. If a Swiss business sells in the United States, check whether it operates in the sectors mentioned: pharmaceuticals, machinery or watchmaking. With a divided Congress, distinguish existing tariffs from the possibility of new measures; with a confirmed Republican majority, consider the possibility of further escalation.
4. If you have expenses in the United States, observe the dollar-franc exchange rate. A weak dollar makes travel and purchases less expensive; for an exporter, however, it can reduce revenue after conversion into francs. For foreign exchange, comparatore CHF/EUR can be used.
5. Keep energy and markets separate. For fuel and heating, look first at geopolitical tensions and the trend in oil prices. For investments, consider the 100 days following the vote without stopping at the result alone: over the long term, earnings, inflation and central-bank decisions matter. A contested outcome can increase tensions and volatility.
### The final check After placing the result in one of the three scenarios, do not automatically combine the dollar, energy and stock market into a single signal. Lombard Odier's indications on foreign exchange, Clientis's on fuel and heating, and VP Bank's reading of the markets concern distinct channels. Separating them avoids using the movement of a single item as a measure of the entire Swiss economy.
To turn the analysis of exchange rates and expenses into a personal check of disposable income, use calcolatore stipendio.

## Key facts - Outcome → failed popular initiative - Threshold → 100 thousand signatures - Deadline → 18 months - Signatures indicated by the committee → 117'500 - Invalid signatures → almost 20 thousand - Verification → July and August - Source of outcome → Federal Gazette - Proposal → no permits for installations on buildings and structures
## The collection stops in Bern
More than 117 thousand signatures were not enough. The popular initiative For solar installations exempt from authorization failed because the 18-month deadline set for collecting the 100 thousand required signatures expired without the target being reached. This is reported in the Federal Gazette, with the signature of the Federal Chancellery.
The initial figure seemed to exceed the threshold. The sponsoring committee's website stated that 117'500 people had signed the constitutional amendment text. Verification, however, reduced that number: checks carried out in July and August revealed that almost 20 thousand signatures were invalid.
Contacted by Keystone-ATS, Roland Weiss, one of the initiative's promoters, confirmed the anomaly. «Our lawyer is currently clarifying the circumstances,» he explained. Weiss added that the committee was trying to understand how such a high number of invalid signatures could have been reached, despite the involvement of entities specialized in collecting signatures.
### The proposed constitutional amendment
The text aimed to introduce a new constitutional article on solar installations installed on buildings and structures. The proposed rule would have excluded the need for a building permit both inside and outside historic centers and protected landscapes.
The exemption would not have been absolute: the text provided for exceptions for installations placed on cultural monuments of national or cantonal importance and on historic sites, where a building permit could have been issued under certain conditions.
The failure of the collection therefore closes the procedure without the constitutional amendment requested by the committee. The source does not link the outcome to a decision on the installations' technical content: it reports that the threshold was not reached after verification of the signatures and the promoters' request for legal clarification. The report contains no estimate of costs or savings; a separate overview of household expenses is available at costo della vita in Svizzera. ## The difference between signatures and text
The practical point for anyone following Swiss politics is to distinguish between the number announced by the committee and the outcome of the verification. The website indicated 117'500 signatures, while the check in July and August excluded almost 20 thousand signatures. The threshold was 100 thousand signatures within 18 months. The failure therefore shows that the gross collection figure did not match the result needed to proceed with the initiative.
The second element is the scope of the exemption. The text called for a new constitutional provision for solar installations on buildings and structures, without a building permit inside and outside historic centres and protected landscapes. The issue therefore concerned not only the collection of signatures: it also defined where the exemption would apply and which exceptions would remain.
### What the proposal would have changed
| Situation provided for | Effect indicated | |---|---| | Installation on a building or structure | No building permit | | Inside or outside historic centres and protected landscapes | Exemption from the building permit | | National or cantonal cultural monument, or historic site | Permit possible under certain conditions |
The presence of exceptions made the framework more complex. A cultural monument of national or cantonal importance, as well as a historic site, would have remained under a regime in which a building permit could be granted under certain conditions. The source does not specify what those conditions were and does not describe the administrative procedure: it is therefore not possible to turn the proposal into a technical checklist for a construction site.
Following the failure, the concrete result is that the exemption described by the committee is not introduced through this initiative. This point is also relevant to avoid overinterpreting the announcement of 117'500 signatures: that was the figure indicated on the website, but the verification found almost 20 thousand invalid ones. The Federal Chancellery recorded the outcome in the Federal Gazette, while the promoters said they wanted to clarify the circumstances.
Since the source does not quantify costs or savings, any economic calculation would be extraneous to the report. For a separate personal check, calcolatore stipendio can be used.

The news makes it possible to follow the dossier through a simple sequence, without attributing to the initiative an effect it did not produce. The starting reference is the Federal Gazette, where the Federal Chancellery recorded that the target had not been met. From there, one can distinguish the formal outcome from the content of the proposal.
### Four useful checks
1. Check the deadline. The period was 18 months and the required threshold was 100 thousand signatures. The deadline expired without the target being met.
2. Separate the figures. The committee's website indicated 117'500 signatures; the July and August verification found nearly 20 thousand invalid signatures. The reported number and the verified result should not be treated as equivalent.
3. Read the scope. The proposal concerned installations on buildings and structures, inside or outside historic centers and protected landscapes. The possible exception for cultural monuments of national or cantonal importance and historic sites must then be considered, where the permit could have been granted under certain conditions.
4. Follow the clarifications. Roland Weiss reported that the legal counsel is clarifying the circumstances and that efforts are being made to understand the origin of the invalid signatures, even after specialized parties intervened. This is the only development following the verification reported by the source.
For anyone considering an installation, the practical conclusion is cautious: the text of the initiative described an exemption, but the initiative failed. Therefore, no automatic authorization can be inferred from this collection. The news offers no other technical steps regarding the installation; its scope remains the outcome of the collection, the constitutional proposal and the clarifications announced by the promoters. ## TL;DR - Trasporti’45 envisages 50 billion by 2045 - The first package is worth 11 billion in 2027 - The railway has a shortfall of 10 billion - The Government proposes extending the VAT surcharge
## Key facts - Plan → Trasporti’45 - Investments → around 50 billion francs by 2045 - First package → 11 billion, to be submitted to Parliament in 2027 - Second proposal → 2031 - Rail network → 10 billion short of the 24 billion needed
Around 50 billion francs for road and rail transport by 2045: that is the scale of Trasporti’45, the plan with which the Federal Council is bringing railways, motorways and urban agglomeration traffic together for the first time. The proposal was met with a barrage of criticism during the consultation process.
Political parties, associations and cantons are challenging both the financing and the choice of priorities. The project is based on an expert report by the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich and provides for a first package worth 11 billion, which the Federal Council intends to submit to Parliament at the beginning of 2027. A second proposal is planned for 2031.
### The rail network in the project
The rail plan includes upgrading the Bienne–Lausanne/Geneva line, a direct connection between Neuchâtel and La Chaux-de-Fonds, and the expansion of Geneva Cornavin station. The construction of a second track and a tunnel between Morges and Perroy will instead be included in the 2031 proposal.
The government also plans to increase the frequency of services between Bern and Zurich, Bern and Lucerne, and Basel and Zurich. Work is also planned for the first phase of Lucerne’s through station and for the Grimsel Tunnel. Several opponents are nevertheless calling for the latter to be excluded from the first proposal, considering the planned funding too high.
Rail funding remains the most sensitive point: developing the network through 2045 requires 24 billion francs, and ten billion are missing. To close the gap, the Federal Council proposes retaining the temporary VAT surcharge beyond 2030, amounting to 0,1 percentage points, and allocating it to the Railway Infrastructure Fund. FFS, UTP and CTSO broadly support the project but are calling for more resources for rail. The guide to mezzi pubblici is also available for following the issue from the national mobility perspective. For Western Switzerland, the difference is particularly visible. The Bienne-Lausanne/Geneva upgrade, the Neuchâtel-La Chaux-de-Fonds line and the expansion of Cornavin are among the selected projects. Morges-Perroy, by contrast, is placed in the 2031 message. The CTSO and OuestRail are calling for a stronger role for the east-west axis, while the Associazione traffico e ambiente maintains that the region has been overlooked and calls for Morges-Perroy to be brought forward to 2027.

The second front concerns VAT and the Railway Infrastructure Fund. PS, Verdi, PLR and Centro support extending the 0,1-point surcharge beyond 2030, but call for greater transparency regarding the fund’s accounts. UDC opposes it. UTP also proposes that repayment of the debts of the Public Transport Fund, amounting to 4 billion francs, remain suspended until 2045.

1. **Mark the timeframe.** The plan concerns investments envisaged by 2045 and includes road, rail and agglomeration transport. This avoids treating each individual project as an isolated decision.
2. Divide the deadlines. The first package, worth 11 billion francs, is to be submitted to Parliament at the beginning of 2027. The second dispatch is expected in 2031. These are the two points in time to keep separate when assessing the projects.

4. Check which projects are contested. The Grimsel tunnel has already been approved in the project, but numerous opponents are calling for its removal from the first dispatch. Morges-Perroy is planned for 2031, while ATA is calling for it to be brought forward to 2027.
5. Read the figures and positions together. Rail needs amount to 24 billion, with a shortfall of ten. The Federal Council’s proposal is to extend the 0,1 percentage-point VAT surcharge beyond 2030; PS, the Greens, PLR and Centre support it, while the UDC opposes it. FFS, UTP, CTSO and the cantons add different requests or reservations.

## TL;DR - In September, confidence falls to -35,8 points. - The figure decreases by 3,0 points compared with August. - Job security moves to -60,6. - The past prices sub-index rises to 129,3.
## Key facts - Period → September - General indicator → -35,8 points - Change compared with August → -3,0 points - 2023-2026 average → -37,3 - Expected economic development → from -36,4 to -42,5 - Job security → from -54,3 to -60,6 - Prices expected over the next twelve months → from 113,3 to 115,6 - Sample → larger in Ticino
## The September figure In September, the general indicator of Swiss consumer confidence reached -35,8 points. Compiled on the basis of a survey by the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), the figure records a decrease of 3,0 points compared with August's value of -32,8 points, the first since last March.
Year on year, the index records a contraction of 0,7 points, but remains slightly above the 2023-2026 average, at -37,3. The monthly decline therefore does not erase the comparison with that average benchmark.
### The signals accompanying the average The sub-index relating to expectations for the country's economic development fell from -36,4 to -42,5, placing it well below the multi-year average of -34,3. Personal financial situation also deteriorated: the reference to recent months fell from -38,8 to -42,3, while the one for the coming months moved from -29,6 to -31,0.
The time for major purchases is considered less favourable, with the corresponding value moving from -26,3 to -27,3. The sharpest change concerns job security, which fell from -54,3 to -60,6. This figure remains much lower than the average of the last three years, at -34,7.
The survey thus shows a monthly deterioration in expected economic conditions, personal finances, purchases and job security. Price indicators, on the other hand, remain positive and at high levels.
The indicator for past price developments rose from 122,5 to 129,3; the one for expectations over the next twelve months from 113,3 to 115,6. For the next five years, the figure instead fell from 109,2 to 105,8, while remaining very high. ## How to read the deterioration The overall value is a summary. To understand which areas are changing in consumers' perception, it is necessary to separate the personal financial situation, propensity for major purchases, employment and prices.
| Area observed | August | September | Reading | |---|---:|---:|---| | Financial situation in recent months | -38,8 | -42,3 | more negative assessment | | Financial situation in the coming months | -29,6 | -31,0 | more negative assessment | | Time for major purchases | -26,3 | -27,3 | less favorable time |
The comparison between the two financial horizons shows that the assessment of recent months remains lower than that of the coming months, but both decline compared with August. It is therefore not only an assessment of the past: expectations for the following months also become more cautious. The same applies to major purchases, whose sub-index falls in the monthly comparison.
### Prices and time horizons The section on prices requires a separate reading. The indicator on past developments rises from 122,5 to 129,3, while the one on expectations for the next twelve months rises from 113,3 to 115,6. The value referring to the next five years instead moves in the opposite direction, from 109,2 to 105,8, while remaining at very high levels.
The source specifies that the price scale produces positive balances when the majority of consumers perceive a price increase. The values should therefore be read as a measure of the perception captured by the survey, without isolating a single time horizon. To complement the price picture with a practical reading of costo della vita in Svizzera, it is advisable to keep the past figure, the expectation for twelve months and that for five years separate.
This distinction also helps explain why a single index does not exhaust the result of the survey: the assessment of personal finances, that of purchases and price expectations can move with different intensity in the same month.

To follow it in an orderly manner, readers can apply the same procedure each time and compare the new values with those from the previous month and with the averages indicated in the survey.
### The reading procedure 1. Identify the reference month and note the general confidence climate index. The survey has been conducted since 1972: in the past it was quarterly, whereas more recently it has been monthly.
2. Distinguish the four subindices of the general indicator: the economic prospects for the coming months, the financial situation over the past months, expectations regarding the financial situation in the coming months, and whether the current moment is favorable for major purchases.
3. Consider the response scale for the fourteen questions. The options range from «much better» (+2 points) to «much worse» (-2), passing through «better» (+1), «no change» (0), and «worse» (-1).
4. Remember how each subindex is created: for each question, the simple arithmetic mean of the responses is calculated and then multiplied by 100. The general index is the mean of the four subindices indicated in the previous point.
5. Read the other signals separately, including job security and prices, without confusing them with the four values used to calculate the general indicator. The sample is deliberately larger in Ticino to ensure fair regional representation.

The monthly comparison shows the most recent movement; the multi-year averages, on the other hand, serve to place it in relation to the benchmarks reported by the source.

### The photograph of the convictions Last year 7,956 people were convicted of theft in Switzerland. It is the central data of the new statistics on criminal sentences from the Confederation, which places thefts alongside road crimes among the categories that collect a large part of the convictions. The data was reported by SRF. The shortening of the days marks the start of the apartment burglary season.
ZHAW criminologist Dirk Baier considers the figure high, but not unexpected. In the SRF «Tagesschau», he defined theft as a significant and often underestimated area of ​​crime.
> In essence, theft represents a significant area of ​​crime, but it often remains underestimated.
Crime statistics also show that two thirds of crimes are property crimes. Examples include bicycle theft, bag theft and burglary.
### Nationality and residence From 2024 the statistics indicate the nationality of those convicted for each crime. In the case of the thefts, around 1,500 convicted people were Swiss, while more than 80% had foreign passports. Among the nationalities particularly represented are those of Algeria and Romania. Furthermore, approximately two-thirds of those convicted with foreign passports are not part of the permanent resident population.
Finally, the source distinguishes two groups indicated by Baier: asylum seekers and criminal tourists. For the former, it recalls a situation that may include few prospects and little money; for the latter it talks about people who arrive in Switzerland knowing that objects are not always well protected and that attention may be insufficient. According to the SEM, the Confederation and the cantons have set up a taskforce for the asylum sector. With regard to repeat offenders, the taskforce uses every instrument provided by law to detain them until their departure. However, the SEM specifies that only a small minority of asylum seekers commit crimes. The Federal Council expects further tightening of the asylum procedure. ## Three filters for reading the statistics

The source places thefts and traffic offenses among the largest categories of convictions, but does not turn the number of people convicted of theft into a general total for crime.
